# CI and staging deployment

The 2026-10-06 capacity failure investigation, local before/after browser measurements, preserved gates and verification limits are recorded in [the performance follow-up](../docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-06-ci-capacity-performance.md). Full workflow duration must be measured on a successful Ubuntu run; local smoke results do not establish target capacity.

เพิ่มเติมสำหรับงานปรับปรุงแพลตฟอร์ม: CI สร้างและเผยแพร่ `postgres-backup` เป็น image ที่หก พร้อมซ้อมกู้ฐาน/เอกสาร/ค่าตั้งในชุดแยกหลัง regression เดิม แต่ auto deploy ยังคงอัปเดตเพียงห้า application images ผู้ดูแลต้องตรวจความเข้ากันได้และเลือก `POSTGRES_IMAGE` ผ่าน Coolify โดยตรง ห้ามตีความผล recovery fixture ว่าปลายทางสำรองของบริษัทหรือเวลา RPO/RTO จริงผ่านแล้ว

`CI and staging / verify` runs on pull requests and main in an isolated GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runner. It installs the frozen lockfile, builds shared packages, checks types and unit tests, builds six images (API, worker, web, MQTT, certbot and postgres-backup), tests managed MQTT startup, real TLS/ACLs and certificate reload, tests certificate lifecycle with mocked ACME/DNS calls, starts disposable PostgreSQL/Redis/MQTT/S3/API/worker/web containers, migrates and runs the explicit manual-user fixture command twice, and runs real HTTP and Chromium E2E. All five application roles log in; API authorization, school isolation, durable telemetry, duplicate ingestion before and after an API restart (including aggregate counts), persisted CSV reports, and desktop/mobile UI are checked. No test connects to staging. The stack and its database are removed even on failure. Only test logs and screenshots are uploaded, not account fixtures.

Only successful main runs in `nateekarni/solar-roof` publish the **same tested image IDs** to GHCR as commit-SHA tags. The deployed references include registry SHA256 digests; tags are for discovery only. The successful publish step lists all six `*_IMAGE` digest assignments in the GitHub Actions job summary for copying into Coolify. The web image uses the same-origin proxy, with no staging URL baked into the browser bundle. GitHub checkout does not persist credentials. The GHCR token is supplied only to the publication step. Pull requests cannot access staging environment secrets or run deployment.

## CI browser preparation and phase timings

The Ubuntu verification job runs the browser in a separate CI-only container using Playwright 1.63.0, matching the installed web workspace package. It pulls `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.63.0-noble@sha256:bc6ab0d6d44ff4826e4cb8c1e6d801e185bfc42bb0753f8e2a30efc70db054c7` for `linux/amd64`; the digest was verified against the registry manifest. The image supplies Chromium and its OS libraries; startup installs the exact `playwright@1.63.0` npm server package. Package and image versions must be updated together. A mismatch fails before pulling.

`scripts/ci/browser-server.sh start` uses a unique run/attempt/job name and ownership label, host networking, host IPC and an init process. The server binds only `127.0.0.1:13999`; readiness uses a real Playwright connection and is bounded to 60 seconds. The preparation step has a five-minute limit, including registry and npm access. `CI_BROWSER_WS_ENDPOINT=ws://127.0.0.1:13999/` is exported only after readiness for integration and platform browser suites. The client passes Chromium's supported localhost-to-IPv4 resolver launch argument, preserving existing localhost cookie origins on the host network. `run-server --unsafe` permits this argument on the loopback-only CI listener. Local tests keep their ordinary Chromium launch unless this CI endpoint is explicitly configured. No production image or deployment configuration includes the browser service.

Always-run cleanup checks the ownership label, captures `test/artifacts/browser-server.log`, and removes only that browser container; existing fixture cleanup remains in each suite. Browser logs join the uploaded test evidence. Pull/start/readiness failures are reported by browser preparation, independently of application suite failures.

The job summary records UTC start/end timestamps, elapsed seconds and exit status for browser preparation, application image build, integration, platform regression, recovery, capacity and GHCR publication. The timing wrapper preserves failing commands' exit status, so publication still requires all existing gates. Skipped phases have no timing row; a runner forcibly terminating the process can prevent its final row from being recorded. Queue time and optional Coolify deployment are outside these verification phase durations. Application image build, integration, platform regression, recovery, capacity and publication have individual limits of 10, 8, 15, 12, 10 and 10 minutes respectively, with the existing 45-minute verification limit retained. These bounds expose stuck phases without relaxing their assertions. Recovery emits fixed phase names and Compose operation/service start/end timestamps and status; command arguments, SQL and captured successful output are excluded from progress logs. Its intentional 190-second backup pause and all restore/refusal gates remain intact.

Performance validation remains pending: no complete Linux browser run or three comparable main/manual workflow runs were dispatched for this change. Collect at least three successful equivalent runs, including a cold browser-image pull, report each phase duration and the median, and compare against a completed baseline before claiming acceleration. Record queue and Coolify deployment separately. The supplied failed run from 2026-10-06 spent approximately 21m03s installing browser dependencies, 4m21s building images, 1m25s in integration, 7m18s in platform regression, 5m22s in recovery, and 2m10s in capacity (step-start boundaries, including transition overhead). It reached evidence upload after about 44m39s and did not publish. Excluding the old browser installation still leaves about 23m36s: a 10–15 minute verification/publication target is unsupported by this baseline. Browser-container preparation and the capacity implementation need new measurements; there is no verified end-to-end speedup yet. If preparation hits five minutes, diagnose registry/npm access before adding caching.

## Deployment layout

For new pilot deployments, use separate [website](../docs/runbooks/coolify-web-first-deployment-th.md) and [MQTT](../docs/runbooks/coolify-mqtt-deployment-th.md) resources. Keep `STAGING_DEPLOY_ENABLED=false` and deploy those resources manually using CI digests. The current automated deployment helper supports only the combined `docker-compose.staging.yml` layout; it does not orchestrate split resources or update POSTGRES_IMAGE. The one-time setup below is for that combined layout.

## One-time setup

1. Protect `main`: require pull requests and successful `verify`; disallow force pushes. `main` is staging. Do not configure `pull_request_target` execution of PR code.
2. Create a GitHub environment named `staging`, restrict deployment branches to `main`. No human approval is required for ordinary successful main runs.
3. Set repository variable `STAGING_DEPLOY_ENABLED` to `false` while configuring the first deployment. This keeps CI/publication working before Coolify exists. Once setup is complete set it to `true`; run the workflow on main once to deploy, then subsequent successful main pushes deploy automatically.
4. Create a Coolify **Git-backed Docker Compose application**, repository `nateekarni/solar-roof`, branch `main`, compose path `/infra/docker/docker-compose.staging.yml`. Configure the required secrets/settings documented beside that compose file. The repository is public, but new GHCR packages start private. For UI-only pulls, the package owner must deliberately make each of the six packages public in GitHub package settings after reviewing the published contents, or use registry access already provisioned by the company. This workflow does not change package visibility. Follow the staging runbook for GitHub and Coolify UI steps.
5. **Disable Coolify Auto Deploy on push and preview deployments before enabling CI deployment.** Remove old unauthenticated/manual deployment webhooks. GitHub Actions is the only deployment writer; do not run manual deployments concurrently. The helper also explicitly disables push and preview deployment every run.
6. In the GitHub `staging` environment configure variables `COOLIFY_URL` (HTTPS origin, no `/api/v1` suffix), `COOLIFY_APPLICATION_UUID`, `STAGING_WEB_URL` (public HTTPS origin, normally `https://solar.fowir.com`). Add secret `COOLIFY_API_TOKEN` with Coolify application read/write and deployment permissions restricted to the staging team/resource where supported. Never put this token in repository files, URLs, or frontend variables. Restrict API access to the runner/network policy suitable for your Coolify installation.
7. Configure DB/storage/JWT secrets before deployment. There is no automatic bootstrap user service. After migration, run `pnpm --filter @solar/api db:create:user` explicitly in the API terminal for each role as described in [manual users](../docs/runbooks/coolify-manual-users-th.md). No demo seed data is loaded and rerunning preserves compatible existing passwords. Configure MQTT accounts/TLS/Cloudflare token only when installing the managed broker.

## Deployment contract and failure recovery

Before any API request, the helper validates all five registry-specific immutable digest references, including `MQTT_IMAGE` and `CERTBOT_IMAGE`. Before mutation, CI rejects stale commits that no longer equal main. The helper verifies the application's UUID, repository, main branch, compose build pack and staging compose path; it rejects an already active deployment. The helper PATCHes the application's tested `git_commit_sha`, disables raw push deployment, updates `API_IMAGE`, `WORKER_IMAGE`, `WEB_IMAGE`, `MQTT_IMAGE`, `CERTBOT_IMAGE` via the authenticated bulk environment API, then POSTs `/deploy`. It polls the returned matching deployment UUID, rejects failed/cancelled deployments, and verifies the final commit equals the tested SHA. Finally CI probes web login and web health. The private API readiness check runs inside the Coolify stack; no public API port is needed. It never prints API response bodies/tokens, follows redirects with credentials, or retries deployment-triggering POSTs.

Both workflow and staging deployment concurrency have `cancel-in-progress: false`: a new push cannot kill a migration. A timeout does not cancel the Coolify deployment. Inspect Coolify and wait for the active deployment to stop before retrying. Failed readiness leaves the job red; it is not a successful release. Database rollback is never automated. For application rollback use a previously tested commit and its five digest references after checking schema compatibility; back up before migrations that cannot be reversed. Keep deployment access limited to this workflow to prevent mutable configuration races.

Verified API references: [application update](https://coolify.io/docs/api/endpoints/applications/update-application-by-uuid), [bulk environment update](https://coolify.io/docs/api/endpoints/applications/update-envs-by-application-uuid), [deploy](https://coolify.io/docs/api/endpoints/deployments/deploy-by-tag-or-uuid), [deployment status](https://coolify.io/docs/api/endpoints/deployments/get-deployment-by-uuid). These are application endpoints; `docker_compose_raw` is not part of the documented application PATCH schema, so this workflow deploys the compose file from the pinned commit.

Local equivalents: `node --test scripts/ci/*.test.mjs`, build `solar-api:ci`, `solar-worker:ci`, `solar-web:ci`, `solar-mqtt:ci`, `solar-certbot:ci` from their matching Dockerfiles. Run the managed-image Python unit tests shown in the workflow, then `bash infra/docker/mosquitto/managed-smoke.sh`, `bash infra/docker/mosquitto/smoke.sh` and `bash scripts/ci/integration.sh`. `bash infra/ci/managed-staging-smoke.sh` also boots the actual staging Compose with a synthetic certificate fixture, checks manual account creation and full stack health, then removes only its disposable project and named volumes. No certificate test uses production secrets or makes real ACME/Cloudflare requests. They require Docker, pnpm, and Playwright Chromium. CI accounts and passwords are deliberately limited to the disposable `solar_readiness` database and localhost ports.
